title: S&P 500 Earnings Beats Hit Five-Year Highs as Consumers Absorb Surging Costs
excerpt: Corporate America is posting its strongest profit season since 2021, driven by AI spending and soaring energy margins, even as gasoline prices above $4 a gallon and rising inflation squeeze household budgets.
body:
• S&P 500 companies reporting Q2 results are beating earnings estimates at a rate not seen in five years, with total profits up over 40% year-over-year for early reporters.
  • AI infrastructure spending, soaring energy margins, and resilient consumer demand are driving the strongest annual profit growth since 2021.
  • Consumers face mounting pressure from gasoline prices above $4 a gallon, a savings rate near four-year lows, and looming Fed rate hikes — a widening gap between corporate windfalls and household strain.

America's largest corporations are delivering a second-quarter earnings season that Wall Street is calling historically strong — even as the consumers who power two-thirds of the economy wrestle with rising fuel costs, stagnant real wages, and a shrinking savings cushion.

Of the 81 S&P 500 companies that have reported so far, total earnings have surged 40.6% from the same period last year on 13.3% higher revenues, according to Zacks Investment Research. A remarkable 91.4% beat earnings-per-share estimates while 81.5% topped revenue forecasts — both matching five-year highs last reached in the third quarter of 2021.

"It's very, very rare that you have this strong of a market, but earnings are even stronger."

— Mark Hackett, Chief Market Strategist, Nationwide

What Is Driving the Profit Surge

Three forces have converged. First, the artificial intelligence infrastructure boom continues to funnel massive capital into semiconductor makers and cloud providers. The technology sector's profit growth is expected to reach 65.5% in the quarter, according to LSEG IBES data, with Nvidia and Micron leading the charge.

Second, the energy sector is posting staggering numbers. ExxonMobil reported $14.5 billion in second-quarter profit — roughly $160 million a day — more than doubling its year-earlier haul, according to CNN. Chevron posted $12.1 billion, quadrupling its result from the same period last year. Global oil prices have climbed more than 40% year-to-date as the US-Iran conflict disrupts supplies and wipes out an estimated six to seven million barrels of refining capacity daily.

Third, broad-based strength extends beyond the headline sectors. Companies ranging from General Motors and AT&T to regional banks have comfortably topped consensus estimates, and management commentary across industries has offered reassuring reads on underlying demand, according to Zacks.

For the full second quarter, S&P 500 companies are expected to report aggregate earnings growth of 23.4% year-over-year, per LSEG IBES — well above the 15.2% growth expected at the start of the year. Full-year 2026 estimates now call for a 26.4% earnings increase, which would be the strongest annual performance since 2021.

The Consumer Squeeze

The flipside of corporate prosperity is the pressure on households. Average gasoline prices have risen back above $4 a gallon amid renewed Middle East hostilities, according to Reuters. The Iran war has cost American consumers more than $76 billion in the form of higher gasoline and diesel prices, according to Brown University's Climate Solutions Lab.

The household savings rate has dropped to a four-year low of about 3.0%, with wages barely keeping pace with inflation. Lower-income families, who spend a larger share of their budgets on energy, are disproportionately hit.

"We expect that higher energy prices will erode household spending power for the rest of the year, particularly for lower-income households that spend a larger share of their budget on energy."

— Joseph Briggs, Economist, Goldman Sachs

Even President Trump, a traditional ally of the oil industry, has warned companies that gasoline prices "better start going down a lot faster," instructing the Justice Department to investigate pricing.

What It Means for Indian-American Investors

For Indian Americans with significant stock-market exposure — and the community's equity participation rate has grown steadily — the earnings-driven rally is a tailwind. The S&P 500 has gained 9% in 2026, and the forward price-to-earnings ratio has actually moderated from 22.2 at the end of 2025 to 20.1, suggesting the advance is earnings-backed rather than purely speculative, according to LSEG Datastream.

The AI spending wave also benefits Indian IT services firms such as TCS, Infosys, and Wipro, whose US clients are ramping up technology budgets. Jeff Buchbinder, chief equity strategist at LPL Financial, told Marketplace that non-tech earnings growth could reach the "high teens" this quarter, broadening the opportunity set beyond the Magnificent Seven.

That said, rising living costs — from the gas pump to groceries — are biting into disposable income for diaspora households just as they are for the broader US population. Economists at Goldman Sachs expect the savings rate to edge up to 3.5% by year-end as households become more cautious.

What to Watch

The coming weeks will be critical. Apple, Microsoft, Amazon, and other mega-cap names are still to report. Analysts caution that the elevated bar makes disappointments riskier. The Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates as soon as September to combat inflation, which could slow consumer spending further and test whether corporate profit resilience can hold.
nri_angle: Indian-American investors benefit from an earnings-driven stock rally while Indian IT firms stand to gain from the AI infrastructure spending powering tech profits, though rising energy and living costs weigh on household budgets.
author: Diaspora Desk
